event.details: Mārkaṇḍeya introduces the future eighth Manu. Suratha of Caitra’s line loses to hostile kings, returns to his own city and resumes ruling his own territory, then suffers renewed enemy attack. His powerful corrupt ministers seize treasury and army even in his city. Riding away under a hunting pretext, he reaches Medhas’s hermitage yet worries about kingdom, elephant, servants and treasure.
event.outcome: Suratha remains attached after dispossession.
event.title: Suratha remains attached after dispossession.

event.details: Suratha asks the distressed merchant his identity. Samādhi says wife, sons and kinsmen expelled him for wealth; he still worries about their welfare. Suratha questions this affection; Samādhi admits knowledge has not made him unloving.
event.outcome: Their shared attachment becomes the question.
event.title: Their shared attachment becomes the question.

event.details: They approach Medhas respectfully. Suratha asks why discrimination does not end attachment. Medhas cites hungry birds feeding young and explains Mahāmāyā’s power over even knowers; propitiated, she also grants liberating knowledge. Suratha asks her origin, nature and activity.

event.cause: Indra’s attraction during the festival and encounter with Durvasas.
event.details: Dakṣa requests origins and battles of eight incarnations; Mudgala begins Vakratunda. Indra’s annual accession festival assembles the named gods, sages, attendants and musicians recorded in mud-e-festival-roster. Rambhā’s performance and ball play enthrall Indra, who closes it prematurely. After forest play with Rambhā, seeing Durvāsas makes him leave her and bow; his seed falls on earth. He returns home, repeatedly condemns his distraction and resumes his own dharma. Matsara arises from his seed; Earth nurtures, names and initiates him at five. He studies Vedas with an unnamed teacher, and marries Durbuddhi’s daughter Madakarā.
event.outcome: Matsara reaches adulthood and marriage.

evidence.paraphrase: Indra is attracted to Rambha during his festival, goes with her into a forest, then sees Durvasas and bows after leaving her. His seed falls on the ground; Matsara arises from Indra’s seed. Earth nurtures, names and has him initiated at age five. He studies, then marries Madakara, daughter of Durbuddhi.

event.details: Vakratunda explains creation as play with each being’s own dharma, his indwelling control through Puruṣa and Prakṛti, and conditional impartiality. When gods abandon duty to uproot demons or obstruct austerity, he inspires and grants demons boons against them. When demons abandon duty to uproot gods, he reveals their vulnerable means through the gods or takes form against demons the gods cannot conquer. He remains Brahman in both when they follow duty. Matsara oppressed gods through abandoning his own dharma, so he came against him.
event.outcome: The apparent favoritism is explained as restoring disrupted dharma.

event.details: Vakratunda declines to destroy a surrendered devotee, offers a boon, and promises Matsara’s hymn sovereignty, health, wealth, family and four aims. event.cause: Bhṛgu explains king’s earlier karma.
event.details: Bhṛgu says Somakānta was Kāmanda, late-born only son of wealthy Vaiśya Cidrūpa and charitable Sulocanā at Kolhāra near Vindhya. Parents doted on him and married him to devout Kuṭumbinī; seven sons and five daughters followed. Father died; mother burned with him and went to heaven. Kāmanda squandered inherited wealth with companions, rejected wife’s warning and sold the house; wife went with children to her father.
event.outcome: Family separates after squandered wealth.

event.cause: Kāmanda refuses surrender appeal.
event.details: Kāmanda rejects the appeal, calls it wasted instruction, refuses release and beheads Guṇavardhana with a sharp sword. Bhṛgu declines to count innumerable killings. Old age and illness bring rejection by household, descendants and friends. Through one trusted Brahmin he summons forest sages and offers gifts; they refuse a fallen donor, describing sinful association, then leave to bathe clothed and recite purifying verses.
event.outcome: Killing is followed in old age by rejection of his proposed gifts.

event.cause: Rejected gifts provoke remorse and temple restoration.
event.details: Illness, family neglect and Brahmin rejection lead Kāmanda to remorse. Brahmins identify an ancient Gaṇeśa image in a ruined forest shrine; he spends his wealth rebuilding a four-gated, four-towered decorated temple with groves and reservoirs; wife, sons, friends and kin take the remaining portion of wealth (hṛtam, not a gift). After death Yama’s messengers torture and bring him before Yama and Citragupta. Offered good or evil fruits first, he chooses merit and is reborn as Saurāṣṭra’s king Somakānta, rewarded for temple construction. Bhṛgu explains this by compassion for a suppliant and austerity power.
event.outcome: Merit-first choice explains royal birth; evil fruits remain.

event.cause: Pride follows divine gifts and cosmic vision.

event.details: Dakṣa asks how Brahmā worshipped Vakratunda. Mudgala recalls Gaṇeśa creating five divine lords and empowering them through austerity/boon. Beginning creation without remembering or worshipping Gaṇeśa, Brahmā prides himself on indispensability: without his creation, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śakti and sun lack their functions. Many-eyed/many-faced Vighna hosts batter and toy with him. He relinquishes pride, takes refuge, remembers and hymns Gaṇeśa; the hosts vanish.
event.outcome: Humiliation and recollection remove the immediate obstruction.

event.details: Freed of obstacles, Brahmā propitiates Vakratunda with six-syllable mantra, feeding on air, standing on toe-tip, holding unwavering mental focus. After a divine thousand of austerity, disturbing beings, Vakratunda comes lion-mounted, three-eyed, elephant-faced, four-armed, with noose/goad/boon/fearlessness, Siddhi/Buddhi, Cintāmaṇi, Śeṣa at navel and red body. Brahmā fears the radiance and requests gentleness. Vakratunda softens it, explains the form ordinarily belongs to Svānanda and manifested through Brahmā’s devotion, then offers wishes.
event.outcome: Gentle manifestation prompts Brahmā’s hymn and boon request.

event.details: Wind shakes Brahmā and Dambha manifests from his body-tremor as a great four-armed armed man. Asked identity, he claims birth from Brahmā’s tremor and sonhood, requests name, place and livelihood. Brahmā laughingly names him Dambha because of his boast, permits movement everywhere and enjoyments. Dambha bows and circles him, reaches earth, resents perceived disrespect and vows to remove Brahmā’s pride. He seeks Kavi, receives a mantra, and worships Brahmā foodless on one foot for ten thousand years, disturbing creation. Pleased Brahmā arrives with gods, astonished at his wooden-stillness and offers a boon.
event.outcome: Dambha’s retaliation motive leads to intense worship of his origin deity.

event.details: Offered wishes, Dambha hymns Brahmā as threefold Brahmā/Viṣṇu/Śiva and all creation. He asks three-world rule, no death from five-element beings, no equal in battle, undivided sovereignty with health. Brahmā grants all requested and any contemplated object’s success, then disappears. event.details: Suhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Rukmaketu, Madyapa, Sakopa, Krodhāsura, Kāmāsura, Rāsabhāsura and other chiefs urge conquest as Dambha’s servants. He agrees, summons Śukra and accepts his counsel, then marches with fourfold forces, defeats terrestrial kings and Pātāla Nāgas, and goes to heaven. Indra’s vajra burns and crushes demons and makes them flee; Dambha’s discus fells Indra, arrows harm gods. Recovering Indra flees to live; Dambha sits on Airāvata and Indra’s throne.
event.outcome: Dambha conquers three worlds; Indra abandons his office.

event.details: Indra and gods take refuge in Brahmā, then Viṣṇu and Śiva. Śiva angrily challenges Dambha; forty days of destructive battle follow. Dambha’s arrows fell divine chiefs. Śiva’s trident fells Dambha, who rises immediately and hurls discus, felling Śiva for half a prahara. Regaining consciousness, Śiva flees with gods to the forest. Dambha installs demons in Satyaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Kailāsa, Amarāvatī and other divine cities, then returns to Śobhana ruling three worlds.
event.outcome: Dambha supplants divine offices after reversible defeats on both sides.

event.details: Dambha orders karma destroyed. Demons bind and beat Brahmins, break sacrificial spaces and trees, destroy tīrthas and temples. Some Brahmins die or abandon duties, others flee forests; sacrificial exclamations and social dharma cease. Gods, dependent on ritual food, appeal to Brahmā as creator/provider and giver of fearlessness: without karma and food they face starvation and death.
event.outcome: Suppression of sacrifice provokes divine appeal for rescue.

event.details: Unable to devise rescue, Brahmā advises one-syllable worship of Vakratunda. Gods/sages worship; he meditates on the previously seen Siddhi/Buddhi-bearing form. After a hundred years he sees the speaking form in his heart, then it emerges with Siddhi and Buddhi. Vakratunda says he arose from Brahmā’s meditation, is dhyānaja, and fulfils the former requested sonhood. Brahmā bows and worships all three. The narrative calls him mental son, Siddhi/Buddhi daughters, and describes Vakratunda as with wife/wives (sabhāryaka) while all prepare a hymn.
event.outcome: Promised sonhood is fulfilled by meditation-origin, not womb birth.

event.details: Brahmā with gods/sages hymns the all-form Brahman deity and marvels that the meditated Siddhi/Buddhi-bearing Brahman came out as his son. Brahmā and Brahmins perform birth rites; on day eleven name him Siddhibuddhipati. He plays as a child, Sāvitrī nurses him, and his deeds please mother and father. At two years, with Siddhi/Buddhi, he asks why father dwells sorrowfully in forest. Brahmā tells Dambha’s story. The child promises to destroy Dambha and restore offices, goes lion-mounted with Siddhi/Buddhi near the city, and sends Indra to demand own-dharma, restored sacrificial food and social order. Dambha spares Indra as envoy, otherwise threatens imprisonment, and sets battle on fifth day. Indra reports and is praised.
event.outcome: A new child manifestation offers rescue and attempts conciliation.

event.details: Dambha summons Kavi/Śukra, prostrates, receives a gold seat and asks who Siddhi/Buddhi and their lord are. Śukra explains Siddhi as alluring māyā and people’s pursuit of worldly/otherworldly/Brahman fulfilment, left at Gaṇeśa’s side; Buddhi as knowledge/mind with five citta states and innumerable variants, at his right. Both māyās were formed from the deity’s own limb for play; Svānanda is Brahman and his abode. Brahmā requested sonhood to remove parental bondage; this deity came accordingly. He warns Dambha to surrender because this form will restore dharma and destroy him.
event.outcome: Guru explains the opponent’s identity, powers and manifestation purpose.

event.details: Dambha asks why impartial Gaṇeśa, from whom dharma/adharma arise, protects one and destroys the other. Kāvya explains an ordered world with separate places: greed-driven excess adharma strengthens Asuras and weakens gods, prompting Gaṇeśa to restore dharma; excessive dharma threatens demon root-destruction, so he grants demons boons to restore adharma’s assigned place. Neither party is self/other to him; greed-driven imbalance draws intervention. Dambha meditates privately, concludes that seeking siddhi or welfare while abandoning their lord causes failure, resolves surrender and sleeps fearlessly with Gaṇeśa in his heart.
event.outcome: Doctrinal answer changes Dambha’s decision before battle.

event.details: Dakṣa asks Vāmana’s story. Mudgala introduces Kaśyapa, his senior virtuous wife Aditi, and gods including Indra born to them; opposing demons are also sage’s sons, defeated by Viṣṇu’s varied forms. They seek Kāvya, who advises100 Aśvamedhas with concealed hostility, making Bali Indra and demons celestial enjoyers. Bali, born of Virocana, is Viṣṇu-devoted and dislikes adharma. Yet he begins the first sacrifice remembering Viṣṇu and omitting Gaṇeśa. Vighna decides to consume its ritual fruits, enters Indra’s heart; Indra fears100 sacrifices will replace him and asks Viṣṇu to destroy them. Vighna then enters Viṣṇu’s heart as time-form.
event.outcome: Neglected initial worship creates obstruction through the divine opponents.

event.details: Viṣṇu tells Indra that Aditi and Kaśyapa previously worshipped him intensely for100 years and requested his sonhood; he agreed and will fulfil it now to stop Bali’s sacrifice. Forgetting Bali’s devotion, Viṣṇu is born Vāmana to Kaśyapa in Aditi, but cannot displace mighty Bali. He asks father Kaśyapa for means; receives Vakratunda’s six-syllable mantra, goes to Vidarbha and worships foodless for10 years, meditating Gaṇeśa. Vakratunda appears through mantra/austerity, lion-mounted, four-armed, one-tusked, elephant-faced, red, with Siddhi/Buddhi and noose/goad. Vāmana rises, bows and begins hymn.
event.outcome: Vāmana seeks Gaṇeśa’s aid after initial inability to move Bali.

event.details: After worshipping Vakratunda and bowing to Kaśyapa, Vāmana reaches Bali’s sacrifice. Sages marvel at radiant short Vedic student; Bali rises, bows, worships and offers a gift. Śukra understands purpose and the initial worship omission producing a Viṣṇu-form obstacle. Vāmana asks land for three steps; Bali grants with devotion. Remembering Gaṇeśa, Vāmana becomes Virāṭ, covers heaven with one step and earth with second, demands place for third. Grieving Bali cannot answer; angry Viṣṇu binds him as debtor to a Brahmin and tells him to go to Naraka. Bali realizes his Gaṇeśa omission has brought this treatment even from his chosen Viṣṇu, and turns to Gaṇeśa for rescue.
event.outcome: Bali is bound for unfulfilled third step, then seeks Gaṇeśa.

event.details: Vāmana hymns Gaṇeśa’s supremacy/māyā, begs forgiveness and sacrificial fruit for Bali, acknowledging Bali’s belief in Viṣṇu’s superiority led to omitted worship. Gaṇeśa says he had earlier promised Naraka through Viṣṇu’s hands, but now Bali has taken bodily/mental/verbal refuge and Viṣṇu also petitions. He orders finishing sacrifice with him first; Bali thereby gains all sacrifices’ fruit, but current fruitlessness lets him experience offence. Bali will be Indra after current Indra retires; for now establish him in Pātāla. All approve; Bali completes the final sacrifice placing Gaṇeśa first. Deity vanishes, gods return home; hearing the arc grants wishes.
event.outcome: Sacrifice repaired; Pātāla placement ordered and future Indra office promised.

Deity vanishes, gods return home; hearing the arc grants wishes.

event.details: Asked what Pradhāna does, Śiva says it creates subtle sāttvic Hiraṇyagarbha/dream world, enclosed by subtle principles. Lacking knowledge, Hiraṇyagarbha performs difficult tapas and receives the desired, unspecified boon/capacity. It creates gross rājasic waking world; this also lacks knowledge, performs tapas, receives appearance, worships and gains a boon/capacity. Gross world becomes many three-state worlds; innumerable eggs emerge from Guṇeśa’s pores. The enclosing/enclosed unity is called Prakṛti/Brahma-bindu.
event.outcome: Causal→subtle→gross creation proceeds through distinct tapas/boons.

event.cause: Mukundā’s desire persists after the real prince’s departure.
event.details: Vyāsa asks about Mukundā after hearing Rukmāṅgada’s ascent. She remains consumed by desire, abandons food/water and sleeps exhausted in the forest. Indra knows her longing, assumes Rukmāṅgada’s form and has intercourse with her; she returns home believing the prince was her partner. Indra vanishes. She conceives and bears a beautiful son in the ninth month.
event.outcome: Impersonation yields pregnancy; her belief is explicitly mistaken.

event.cause: Vācaknavi believes the child belongs to his household.
event.details: Birth resounds through earth, sky and directions and startles birds. Vācaknavi leaves his daily rites and, unaware of Mukundā’s conduct, joyfully performs birth rites and donations. After ten days he names the child Gṛtsamada with astrologer Brahmin approval; in the fifth year initiates him and performs four Vedic vows. The boy learns from a single utterance. Vācaknavi, called father in this social/ritual setting, teaches the Vedic Gaṇānāṃ tvā mantra, prescribing steady Gaṇeśa contemplation for success and fame.
event.outcome: Naming, initiation, learning and mantra instruction completed.

event.cause: Boast during learned discussion produces parentage rebuke.
event.details: Gṛtsamada practices mantra/meditation. King Magadha of Magadha, generous, martial and learned, with two unnamed learned ministers and devoted curse/grace-capable wife Ambikā, hosts his father’s śrāddha. Invited sages include Vasiṣṭha and Atri, and Gṛtsamada. His boast in śāstra discussion provokes Atri’s rebuke: ascetic merit earns respect, but alleged birth from prince Rukmāṅgada excludes equal sage-honour. Gṛtsamada flares with rage, others flee, and he threatens to burn the sages by curse if he proves not Rukmāṅgada’s son.
event.outcome: He leaves to interrogate his mother; alleged parentage is attributed speech.

event.details: Ṛcīka sees fierce radiance in his wife and asks about Kṣatriya potency. She admits the exchange; he predicts her brother will be an ascetic, her son a fierce bowman. Afraid, she asks a Brahmin son and threatens her life otherwise. He shifts that quality to her grandson, informs Viṣṇu of the pregnancy and effects it through tapas. Jamadagni is born to him; Rāma, best bearer of weapons, becomes Jamadagni’s son. Gādhi’s queen bears Viśvāmitra in ninth month; Gādhi installs his grown son in the kingdom and leaves for austerity.

event.details: Viśvāmitra abandons kingdom, fasts and repeats Gāyatrī by puraścaraṇa for Brahminhood, scorching the world. event.details: Yājñavalkya applies the example: worship Vighnarāja and abandon pride to become Brahmin. Viśvāmitra asks where pride resides, how to abandon it and how to worship/understand Gaṇeśa. The teacher identifies certainty that one’s own tapas must confer Brahminhood as pride. Practise sincerely but accept the deity’s grant or continued Rājarṣi status, knowing embodied dependence. Abandon competitiveness, think oneself below all Brahmins/ascetics and inwardly honor them. He reproaches Viśvāmitra’s envy: destruction of Vasiṣṭha’s100 sons as by a Rākṣasa, alternate creation for Triśaṅku and attempts on Vasiṣṭha’s life. Without reform even a thousand yugas of tapas ends in death.

story.title: Kāśī, Divodāsa and Śiva’s restored residence
story.completeness_basis: Entire bounded cited Sanskrit arc read; significant named actors, relationships, boons/powers, dialogue and transition checks by author. Independent root review separate.

event.details: After60 rainless years and terrestrial devastation, Brahmā approaches Sūrya-line king Divodāsa, who left rule and performs devotional tapas for liberation. Brahmā asks him to take Kāśī to save life, promising rainfall if he rules. He first refuses, asking liberation; then compassionately accepts on condition earthly rule excludes gods, while gods/heaven, humans/earth and Nāgas/Rākṣasas/Pātāla keep their domains. He will worship Śambhu as a deity; Brahmā agrees and grants Kāśī.

event.details: Brahmā takes Śiva with gods/sages to Mandara to grant Marīci a boon, warning the ascetic will die otherwise. Marīci asks liberation; suffering from tapas he relinquishes life, obtains Śiva’s likeness and reaches Kailāsa. Brahmā then asks Śiva to remain at Mandara, explaining Divodāsa’s condition for drought relief and asking pardon. Śiva agrees with a sigh and stays with Pārvatī/Gaṇas.

event.details: Śiva laments that Avimukta was taken from him and his Viśvanātha title is powerless. Recognizing obstacle and removal of pride, he resolves refuge in Vighnarāja and meditates on Gaṇeśa at the mountain for Kāśī. Personified Kāśī hears his departure, loses pride and meditates on Vighneśa for Śiva. Divodāsa’s righteous reign restores rain, joy and sinless observance of social duties.

event.details: Gods resent loss of earthly sovereignty and scheme against the king. Indra orders Agni to withdraw outward fire; people seek Divodāsa, who assumes fire-form by tapas everywhere on earth. As other gods withdraw he supplies their functions through forms including Vāyu, unknown to the people. Gods ask Brahmā what to do; he sends them to request restored places. They praise Divodāsa, he praises them and restores their offices, remaining in one human body. Agni and others resume their places. The transcription misnumbers sequential63 as33.

event.details: Śiva grieves that the righteous tapas-powered king cannot be displaced. Gods/sages offer to lure citizens by siddhis so their sin falls on king, then Śiva can take Kāśī. Their many forms and siddhis fail for a year because citizens remain righteous. Śiva’s further dispatched Bhairavas, Ādityas, Vasus, sages, Yoginīs and Gaṇas fail. Brahmā is sent and performs ten Aśvamedhas, then becomes quiet.

event.details: Śiva meditates on Vighnarāja for one year, asking freedom from obstacles and separation. Seeing complete humility, Vakratunda manifests lion-mounted, four-armed, noose/goad/boon/fearlessness, red elephant face, great belly, Siddhi/Buddhi, Śeṣa at navel and Cintāmaṇi. Śiva worships/hymns creator/preserver/destroyer and causal/transcendent forms, seeks inseparable Kāśī, and recalls an earlier promise to appear in son-relation on remembrance. Vakratunda promises hymn recitation/hearing gives siddhis, enjoyment/liberation and all other requests, restoring Avimukta meaning.

event.details: With Gaṇeśa’s boon Brahmā resolves creation, enters Janārdana through yogamāyā, hides in him and after a year emerges from his navel-lotus, becoming Viṣṇu’s son under the boon recalled here; the exact grant agency is established separately at1.13.33–37. Meditating on Heramba, his own body releases water filling ten directions; submerged and bewildered, he remembers Vakratunda for rescue. On remembrance he sees a banyan and thumb-sized sleeping Gaṇeśa on a leaf, three-eyed, four-armed, elephant-trunked, large-bellied, Śeṣa at navel, moon/crown/adornments/clothes. The child sprays Brahmā with trunk-water; delighted Brahmā begins a hymn.

event.details: Remembering Gaṇeśa, Brahmā emits Avidyā from body, divided fivefold, red/black/white and deluding the threefold world. Tamas obscures through ignorance/body-interest; Moha produces desires/varied enjoyment-actions; Mahāmoha wrong action/sin for bodily pleasure; Tāmisra produces sickness/poverty and mental/physical affliction; Andhatāmisra produces karmic hell-torments. Avidyā remembers Gaṇeśa and pursues her purpose; Brahmā condemns her and resolves further creation.

event.details: Four sons arise from Brahmā’s body: Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana and Sanatkumāra. Vidyā/jñāna is their mother-form, formless bodha/self nature. Their paths: Sanaka sahaja, Sanandana sama-yoga, Sanātana jñāna-yoga, Sanatkumāra karma-yoga. At Brahmā’s order to create remembering Gaṇeśa they create many yoga paths; displeased Brahmā tells them to stop yoga-creation and they comply.

event.details: Angry at knowledge-creation, Brahmā emits Śambhu as forehead-born son: five faces, three eyes, ten arms, half-female/male, crescent, trident, matted hair and tiger/elephant skins. Crying child asks father for place, names and task. Brahmā names Rudra for crying, Śiva as all-happiness ground, recalls boon giving son-form, assigns eight abodes earth/water/fire/wind/space/moon/sun/consecrated sacrificer and eleven names, and orders creation after Gaṇeśa meditation. Śiva creates countless immortal Rudras. Asked to create birth/death beings, he refuses and stays quiet, called Sthāṇu, celibate/upward-seeded and worshipping Gaṇeśa.

event.details: Ten body-born sons appear: Marīci, Bhṛgu, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada. Ordered to create, they agree and go to forest tapas. Nārada refuses creation, choosing Gaṇanāyaka worship because world is māyā/mithyā; Brahmā insists create first, worship in old age. Nārada questions labour for delusive aims. Brahmā angrily curses Śūdra birth and woman-enjoying Gandharva life; Nārada curses Brahmā to be unworshipped for needless cursing.

event.details: Nārada propitiates Gaṇeśa by one-syllable mantra for100 divine years and requests curse removal after hymn. Gaṇeśa says he cannot falsify father’s curse because his prior boon makes Brahmā truthful. Instead he will teach Nārada as Gandharva so māyā cannot hurt him amid women; then Śūdra birth with renouncer company/knowledge, forest life and Vaiṣṇava path; after that body falls, he again becomes Brahmā’s son Nārada, worships Śambhu and learns Gaṇeśa from Nārāyaṇa to become a loved Gāṇapatya/yoga lord. Gaṇeśa disappears; narrator says Nārada undergoes curse, returns to heaven and is reborn as Śiva-devotee, then Nārāyaṇa teaches him Gāṇapatya devotion.

event.details: Dakṣa asks how Nārāyaṇa taught Nārada. Nārada sees Śaṅkara devotedly worshipping a jeweled Cintāmaṇi/Gaṇeśa image on Kailāsa, tearful and immersed in meditation, then approaches Viṣṇu at Vaikuṇṭha. He asks why Śiva, whom he regards as immutable unmanifest Brahman, worships another, and why Viṣṇu also chants Gaṇeśa’s name. Nārāyaṇa answers Gaṇeśa is yoga-peace, Siddhi/Buddhi lord in Svānanda, sole Vināyaka; the other deities gain siddhi-giving power by devotion and worship for yoga-peace.

event.details: Nārāyaṇa recounts asking Śiva the same question after his daily worship. Śiva explains Buddhi as fivefold mental activity/Prakṛti enjoying fivefold, Siddhi as manifold delusion for whose attainment mind strives, including four aims and Brahman state. Brahman-attainer has no fivefold mind, is yogin non-different from Gaṇeśa. Ga denotes saṃprajñāta, ṇa asaṃprajñāta; Gaṇeśa is their yoga-peace lord. Śiva names himself unmanifest/neti, Viṣṇu sama, and distinguishes bhava-pratyaya’s fivefold/māyā Gaṇeśa and upāya-pratyaya’s māyā-free, while direct Gaṇeśa transcends either and is attained by peace. He urges fivefold-mind abandonment to become Cintāmaṇi; Nārāyaṇa concludes Gaṇeśa grants their offices and Brahman state and is their family deity.

event.details: Gaṇeśa’s boons create five independent unbroken worlds: Śiva/Kailāsa, Viṣṇu/Vaikuṇṭha, Sun/Sauraloka, Śakti/Śaktiloka, Brahmā/Satyaloka. Initially mutual benefactors, they grow envious and claim unique supremacy. Viṣṇu creates body-water, sleeps; algae/creeper then earth develop. Viṣṇu denies deceit, claims supreme preservation enables Brahmā and has no equal.

event.details: Mudgala recounts śiloñcha gleaning and Dvādaśī fast-breaking after a fortnight, gathering a droṇa of food and performing five yajñas. Gods fear his tapas seeks their Indra/Brahmā/Viṣṇu/Śiva offices and send angry Durvāsas to test him. At fast-breaking the sage arrives naked, like a madman, asks alms and is not recognized. Mudgala gives all food; Durvāsas eats the droṇa, smears leftovers on his body and leaves. Mudgala rejoices in feeding the guest and continues fasting. The same guest consumes all food at six fast-breakings; after three months of fasting Mudgala remains unmoved, attributed to prior merit.

He finds Saubhari teaching distress-removing knowledge to disciples among sages, bows, and is welcomed and seated. He asks relief from the verbal wounds of family and friends, heat, cold, hunger and thirst, while admitting he has not become detached from his harsh loved ones.

event.details: The kṣatriya asks the time and procedure, promising practice for relief. Saubhari prescribes Śrāvaṇa’s non-dark fourth through Bhādra fourth, daily sixteen-service worship of an earthen image and Brahmin feeding, promising all wishes. Bhṛgu says Kardama’s former self performs it at Saubhari’s hermitage. At completion, Gaṇeśa’s favour transforms his home into a divine household with servants, cattle and Vedic sound; his adorned wife and children await him. After leaving the teacher he does not recognize the grand house and searches for his former home, until his wife’s messengers bring him in. He recognizes Varada’s power. Bhṛgu attributes his present kingship to the vow.
event.outcome: The past vow transforms his household and is said to cause later kingship.

event.details: Priyavrata’s wives and ministers are introduced. Prabhā wins his preference while Kīrti is rejected. Prabhā’s son receives rites, initiation and a princess’s marriage; the first wife is reduced to service and kicked down.

evidence.paraphrase: Śiva describes wise, righteous and generous Priyavrata, who treats his subjects as sons. His first wife is Kīrti, the other Prabhā; Dhūrta and Kuśala are his ministers, skilled in policy and compared to Ṣaḍānana in valor. Prabhā captivates him. He cannot bear separation from her, scorns Kīrti, ignores her words and gifts and even thinks of her death. Prabhā bears Padmanābhi; the king performs birth rites, names him, initiates him in his fifth year and arranges marriage to a Pañcāla princess. Priyavrata is called lord of Madra. Kīrti, reduced to a servant, comes to massage his feet and is kicked down by her co-wife.

event.details: Kīrti despairs and considers Hari’s aid to Draupadī. Devala teaches Gajānana worship. She worships the Mandāra image with sixteen services and a hymn framed by five-deity non-difference.

evidence.paraphrase: Ashamed and weeping, Kīrti returns home. She thinks of Hari’s rescue of Draupadī through remembrance and considers fasting to death, poison or drowning, but cannot decide. Priest Devala arrives and teaches Gajānana worship that ends distress and fulfills desires. She obtains a Mandāra-made image, bathes and worships. The passage teaches Gaṇeśa’s priority and the non-difference of five divine forms, one Supreme appearing for the world’s benefit; differentiating them brings hell. She performs sixteen services with dūrvā, flowers, gifts and bows. Her hymn identifies the Lord with the world’s cause, named gods, nature, pleasure and pain, sons and wealth, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, all times, refuge, ritual and knowledge, and all mantra and tantra procedures.

event.details: Unable to obtain dūrvā, her friends bring śamī. At year’s end a dream gives unsolicited marital and son grants, predicts fourth-year poison death and Gṛtsamada’s revival, and promises hymn-reading fruits.

evidence.paraphrase: Kīrti worships and sings the hymn daily. Her friends cannot find dūrvā in Śukra month and bring śamī leaves instead. She offers them with the full services and observes a fast under her vow without dūrvā. At year’s end the image speaks in a dream, pleased by the leaves. Kīrti says nothing, so the deity promises a submissive husband, pleasures and a strong son devoted to her, named Kṣipraprasādana. He predicts poison death in the fourth year, revival by Gṛtsamada, long life and righteous rule. Hymn reading gives influence over king and others, progeny, wealth, Vedic learning and stronger intelligence; reading three times daily gives desired ends, firm devotion and final liberation. The deity vanishes; Kīrti wakes tearful and grateful, regarding sight and speech themselves as the highest fruit.

event.details: After completing her vow, Kīrti waits. Prabhā’s illness changes the king’s preference; Kīrti bears the promised son. Jealous Prabhā gives poison, physicians fail, she is expelled and the child dies as his mother takes him into the forest.

evidence.paraphrase: Next morning Kīrti bathes and worships, completes her vow, restores the image to its previous place, honors her priest and awaits the remembered grants while meditating and reciting names. Prabhā develops a bleeding illness through prārabdha and divine will; unsuccessful treatment and her appearance lead the king to reject her. Kīrti’s tapas and Gaṇeśa’s grace bring beauty and the king’s attachment. She bears Kṣipraprasādana; the king gives gifts, stations brāhmaṇas in five directions, performs birth rites and names him. Jealous Prabhā fears his royal priority—the text uses jyeṣṭhaputra—and gives poisoned curd rice. She herself cries the alarm. Physicians diagnose poisoning; medicines and mantras fail, and the king expels Prabhā. Kīrti and friends carry the child into the forest. One yojana from the city he dies. She mourns, faints, recovers and remembers the deity.

event.details: Gṛtsamada hears the grieving mother’s refuge request. He orders transfer of the śamī-worship merit into the child’s hand, and the boy rises. Kīrti reports the messengers’ battle and asks how the sage knew and why the leaf has this power.

evidence.paraphrase: Gṛtsamada, an ascetic and foremost Gaṇeśa devotee, passes and stops compassionately. Kīrti bows and asks him to revive the child born through Gaṇeśa’s grant and named by divine command, explaining her co-wife’s poisoning. After brief meditation, the sage orders her to offer the merit of her unknowing śamī worship into the child’s hand: through that grace he will rise. She transfers the merit; he rises as if sprinkled with nectar and she bows again. Asking how the sage knew and about the leaf’s greatness, Kīrti reports that Gaṇanātha’s messengers fought and drove away Yama’s messengers, revived the child and returned to their Lord. These battle statements belong to her speech; they are not a separately observed narrator scene.

event.details: The revived child cannot pronounce the six-syllable mantra already taught. Kīrti asks an easy, effective formula leading to rule. Gṛtsamada gives his own four-syllable Dhundhirāja name, explains śamī worship and its royal/enemy-destroying benefit, and answers her request for the deity’s identity and history by beginning Durāsada and Divodāsa accounts.

evidence.paraphrase: Kīrti is satisfied with the plant account, but the revived child cannot pronounce his already taught six-syllable mantra. She asks for an easy, quickly effective mantra leading to royal rule. Gṛtsamada promises his own happiness-giving mantra, the four-syllable name Dhundhirāja. He lists divine worshippers seeking their respective cosmic functions, including Janārdana, Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, Sun, Varuṇa, Moon, Yama, Agni, Vāyu, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Śeṣa and celestial groups. Devotional śamī worship will make her son a ruler and destroyer of enemies. She asks the deity’s birth, nature, deeds, name and earlier worship. The sage promises Durāsada’s defeat, the name’s origin and the later Divodāsa account, as heard from Skanda’s teaching to Agastya.

event.details: The sage departs. Mother and son go to the Kāśī festival, offer roadside leaves/flowers, remain fasting and receive the ten-armed vision and boon invitation.

evidence.paraphrase: After Gṛtsamada finishes the Dhundhi account, he receives permission and returns to his āśrama. Kīrti takes her son to Dhundhi’s shrine at Vārāṇasī on a Tuesday Māgha fourth. The festival’s wealth, food, ornaments and offerings obscure the divine face. Thinking herself poor and unable to match these gifts, she offers dūrvā, śamī and Mandāra gathered on the road and asks her son’s advancement. The Lord values their devotion more than wealth. Others leave; mother and son remain fasting. Dhundhirāja appears from the image with ten arms, crown, yellow clothing, tusk and jewels. They are overwhelmed and forget even worship/bowing. He invites a boon and declares the leaves/flowers more pleasing than riches.

story.title: Sāvitrī river curse, goddess śamī tapas and restored gods with river aṃśas

event.details: At Mahābala, the hurried sacrifice neglects Gaṇeśa and Sāvitrī and seats Gāyatrī. Sāvitrī’s curse becomes river forms at the petitioners’ request, including Śiva/Veṇyā and Kṛṣṇa/Kṛṣṇā.

evidence.paraphrase: Gṛtsamada describes Śiva, Girijā, gaṇas and sages at Mahābala in Sahyādri. Brahmā comes with two wives for a sacrifice; Śiva summons Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Mārkaṇḍeya, Nārada, Kapila, Pulaha, Kaṇva, Viśvāmitra, Trita, Dvita and others. Hurrying at the chosen morning time, they forget Vināyaka worship and leave Sāvitrī occupied with household work. They seat Gāyatrī and begin the rites and fire. Angry Sāvitrī declares failure and curses gods and sages to become insentient for seating the unauthorized wife. They request water and river forms instead, with a letter-equivalence phrase, and she assents. Śiva becomes Veṇyā, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇā and the others rivers bearing their names. The passage compares obstacles during Śiva’s destruction of Tripura when Gaṇeśa was neglected.

event.details: Brahmā and the goddesses acknowledge the neglected worship and plan devotion. The women go to the Rāma-established Vakratunda image in Karnāṭaka; his victory is recalled briefly.

evidence.paraphrase: Brahmā is distressed that his sacrifice caused the gods’ river forms and resolves to please Vighnahartā. Pulomajā, Girijā, Chāyā, Kamalā and other goddesses ask why the senior wife and Gaṇeśa were neglected and how to find relief. Brahmā reassures them and prescribes devotion, which he will also perform. They go to Karnāṭaka to a Mandāra-root image installed by Rāma as Vakratunda. The passage reports that its Lord’s boons made Rāma victorious over Rākṣasa leaders and Daśānana and brought him home with his wife. The goddesses begin severe tapas.

event.details: Varied austerities initially fail. Following a sky instruction, all offer śamī leaves and receive the four-armed, TWO-TUSK, mouse-mounted vision with Siddhi and Buddhi.

evidence.paraphrase: The goddesses use name and mantra recitation, lotus and hero postures, fasting, sweeping, circumambulation, bows, standing on one great toe, meditation and hymns. After a long time the Lord is not pleased. They offer flowers, dūrvā, incense, lamps, food, gold, Mandāra and śamī in different ways. A sky voice says he will not be pleased without śamī, so all worship with its leaves. Gajānana appears compassionately: four arms, crown, armlets, necklaces and earrings, long ears, cheeks, TWO TUSKS, Siddhi and Buddhi, mouse mount and yellow garments. Radiant like crores of suns, he receives their joyful prostration and hymn.

event.details: The goddess hymn requests original forms and constant remembrance. Gaṇeśa preserves Sāvitrī’s curse through river portions while restoring gods’ forms and offices. They apologize and worship.

evidence.paraphrase: At Kīrti’s request Gṛtsamada gives the goddesses’ hymn, praising the all-formed inner ruler, infinite power, refuge, many manifestations and weapons, world-protection and grants. They request the watery gods’ original forms and uninterrupted remembrance. Pleased, Gaṇeśa grants their wishes: Sāvitrī’s word cannot be made false, so gods recover original forms and offices while portions remain as rivers. He orders śamī worship, saying a leaf equals offering the world and gives the fruit of a hundred bhāras of gold. The gods actually regain their forms while river portions remain. They ask forgiveness for neglecting the elder wife and deity through delusion, rejoice and worship with leaves.

event.details: Gods install the stone Heramba temple at Supattana; Indra takes the earlier Mandāra image. Divine offices and household joys return. Brahmā performs twelve YEARS of tapas and repeats the sacrifice.

evidence.paraphrase: The Lord accepts and disappears. Gods install a stone image with four arms, trunk and elephant face, called Heramba, and a temple at Supattana for the world’s benefit. They promise all desires through devotional worship, remembrance and bowing. Indra takes the earlier Mandāra image to his city and worships it with his wife. Gods return to their offices, make Mandāra images and worship with śamī, enjoying their spouses and fulfilled desires. After twelve YEARS of tapas, Brahmā pleases Vighneśa and repeats the sacrifice. He worships a Mandāra image with śamī, gold leaves, dūrvā, Mandāra, ketaka and white dūrvā.

event.details: The wasted Sumudrā/caṇḍālī wanders south of the city and sees Gaṇeśa’s temple with trees, birds and observance practitioners seeking wishes, sons, liberation or wealth. On Bhādra fourth, a city-wide Gaṇeśa festival meets a torrential storm. Driven and beaten from houses, she enters the temple holding fire; some beat her there, but yogins restrain them. She lights grass to warm herself. Wind carries one dūrvā sprout onto Gaṇeśa’s head. The cold-fearing donkey enters, and the bull, released from the plough, also comes by providence.
event.outcome: Unintended grass-offering occurs during three cursed beings’ storm refuge.

event.details: The bull and donkey eat her grass and fight with hooves and horns near the deity while people sleep. Dūrvā falls from their mouths onto Gaṇeśa’s trunk and feet, pleasing him. She strikes them with a staff and eats the offerings. People awaken at hoof sounds, beat and expel her with staff, fist, elbow and stones. Fearing contact, they bathe the deity with enchanted tīrtha water and worship afresh. They also beat all three and close the temple doors, leaving the trio without escape.
event.outcome: Further inadvertent offerings and renewed worship arise amid violence.

event.details: Kauṇḍinya recounts Nārada visiting Gaṇeśa after many days. The sage bows, praises the fruitful sight and stands with joined hands. Gaṇeśa holds his hand and seats him. Nārada says he came to report an astonishing matter and would depart after bowing. Gaṇeśa asks him to describe everything before returning to his hermitage.
event.outcome: Nārada receives an explicit invitation to tell the report.

event.details: Nārada reports Janaka of Mithilā as proud, generous and learned in Vedas and Vedāṅgas: he continually feeds and honours Brahmins with ornaments, clothing and gifts, gives wealth to poor, blind and destitute people, and grants petitions. Nārada wonders whether Gaṇeśa’s satisfaction accounts for undiminished wealth. On visiting, Janaka mocks him through pride in Brahman knowledge. Nārada praises Gaṇeśa as giver of the king’s devotional desires, but Janaka claims to be lord, giver, enjoyer, protector, maker, cause and instrument, with none other in three worlds. Angered, Nārada says God alone makes the world, challenges the king’s apparent religious display, and promises evidence soon.
event.outcome: The king’s attributed claims and Nārada’s challenge motivate the later test.

event.details: Having heard the report, Gaṇeśa honours Nārada with arghya, ornaments, flowers and sandal. With permission Nārada goes to Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha. Gaṇeśa comes to Mithilā to test the king’s devotion, wearing a repulsive old Brahmin form with bleeding wounds, flies and missing teeth. He stumbles, faints and falls amid children; people cover their noses and spit. At the royal gate he asks to be announced as an old, hungry Brahmin guest desiring a meal. Janaka orders his admission, observes his filthy clothes, trembling, bleeding and exhaustion, suspects a divine test, and resolves to satisfy him if merit allows.
event.outcome: The narrator identifies the disguised deity; Janaka separately conjectures a divine guest.

event.details: The guest says he came after hearing Janaka’s fame and asks food until fully satisfied, promising the merit of one hundred sacrifices. Janaka takes him inside, honours him and serves tasty food. The guest consumes the entire portion in one mouthful, then a mountain-sized portion in one mouthful, then prepared food sufficient for ten thousand. Rice is put to cook in innumerable vessels and he eats every finished batch.
event.outcome: Successive immense servings fail to satisfy the guest.

event.details: Some advisers conjecture that the guest is a Rākṣasa and gifts to such beings give no merit; others say even the three worlds could not satisfy him and urge offering grain. All palace, city and village grain is gathered and consumed, still without satisfaction. Messengers report none remains; Janaka lowers his head. The guest departs house to house asking food. Residents explain their grain was collected by the king and already eaten by him. He questions how he can leave unsatisfied after hearing Janaka’s unparalleled giving fame. Amid silence he finds the Brahmin home of Virocanā and Triśiras, enters like its owner, and sees no equipment or metal vessels.
event.outcome: Janaka’s resources are exhausted; the test continues in a poor couple’s home.

event.details: The couple sits on bare earth, with sky as covering, avoiding contact with metals. They eat unasked food, use water for their rites and maintain purity. Amid flies and mosquitoes their Gaṇeśa image is worshipped with flowers and leaves in exclusive devotion. The disguised guest says Janaka did not satisfy him and ostentatious action cannot preserve sattva; he asks anything in their house that could satisfy him. The couple wonders how they, poor people, can feed one whom an emperor could not, comparing a drop with rivers unable to fill the ocean. He says even a small devotional gift greatly satisfies him; abundant gifts without devotion or given for display are fruitless.
event.outcome: The guest explains why devotional giving differs from abundance without devotion.

event.details: Śūrasena asks Indra how Brahmā taught Kṛtavīrya the successful Sankaṣṭa vow. Indra recounts the father approaching Brahmā in Satyaloka and asking what people in distress, anxiety, separation from friends, difficult undertakings, or seeking wealth, sons and good fortune should do. Brahmā prescribes the wish-accomplishing vow: daytime bathing with herbs and white sesame, proper intention and Gaṇeśa meditation, and devotional worship with Āgama mantras on dark fourth at night’s moonrise. The king asks the exact worship method.
event.outcome: Brahmā answers a general remedy request and specifies time, preparation and ritual authority.

event.details: After daily rites at moonrise, prepare a clean cow-dung-coated place with a pavilion and honour Gaṇeśa’s seat with kuṅkuma and rice. Set a kalaśa with five gems and a gold vessel; silver, copper or bamboo is permitted when unavailable, and cloth according to ability. Draw the Āgama-prescribed yantra and install a well-formed gold image. Meditate one-tusked, huge, molten-gold-coloured, large-bellied, wide-eyed Gaṇeśa with fire-like eyes, riding a mouse, fanned by Gaṇas, with Śeṣa as sacred thread. Invoke him to remove distress and remain present until the vow ends.
event.outcome: The image/mount/thread are meditation instructions; no actual travel or new birth is inferred.

event.details: The parenthetical ritual alternatives recite Puruṣa as thousand-headed, thousand-eyed and thousand-footed, embracing what has been and will be; Virāj arises, and Puruṣa arises from Virāj. Gods perform sacrifice with Puruṣa as offering, spring as ghee, summer as fuel and autumn as offering-material; gods, Sādhyas and sages worship the primordial sacrificial Puruṣa. From the sacrifice arise the curd-ghee mixture and aerial, forest and village animals, Ṛc/Sāman/metres/Yajus, horses, creatures with teeth on both sides, cattle, goats and sheep. The bodily social formula assigns mouth to Brahmins, arms to Rājanyas, thighs to Vaiśyas and feet to Śūdras. The cosmic formula gives Moon from mind, Sun from eye, wind/breath from ear, Fire from mouth, interspace from navel, heaven from head, earth from feet and directions from ears. The gods bind Puruṣa as sacrificial animal with seven enclosures and twenty-one fuel-sticks; the closing alternative praises ancient Sādhyas in heaven. These are prescribed Vedic recitations, without a new narrated Gaṇeśa birth or universal biological identity assertion.
event.outcome: All named cosmogonic formula roles remain source-attributed ritual assertions.

event.details: Citralekhā had taken Pradyumna’s son away. Grieving and uncertain where or by whom he was taken, Pradyumna hears Rukmiṇī address him as her son. She recalls Śambara abducting him when he was six days old, many years of grief and comparisons with other women’s growing sons, then Lomaśa’s fortunate visit and instruction in Sankaṣṭa-caturthī. She practiced four times; through its favour Pradyumna returned after killing Śambara in battle. She urges him to practice the same vow so he will learn where his son is.

event.details: Brahmā says he too performed the vow desiring creation and produced varied creation through its power. Dhruva is axis of luminary wheel, holding wind-rays and moving stars. These are source cosmography, not modern astronomical measurements.

event.details: Moon three-wheel chariot has 10 jasmine-white horses left/right; star pathways and Dhruva support with waxing/waning. Sun Suṣumna ray replenishes Moon nectar drunk by gods in sequence over half-month. With little fifteenth-part remaining, Pitṛs attend in afternoon and drink for 2 LAVAS; remaining kalā is svadhā nectar issued through rays at amāvāsyā, giving monthly satisfaction. Moon does not perish from nectar drinking; Sun causes waxing/waning. No lava-to-modern-time conversion.

event.details: Below Varāha are purifying/punishing hells Raurava, Tāmisra, Mahāraurava, Andhatāmisra, Sūcīmukha, Lohadaṇḍa, Taptavāluka, Khaḍgapatraka, Lālāsya, Kṛmibhakṣya and many others, where sinners are cooked. event.details: Forest Ṛṣabha performs various tapas and yoga, becomes avadhūta, passes jada/unmatta/piśāca and sahaja states. He follows fourth, unmanifest, neti, delusion-free, independent Śaṅkara Brahman and teaches Śiva wherever he goes. Yoga reveals independence as defect, since Brahman neither depends nor is independent; loses peace, visits Śiva’s abode, receives honor, and is astonished by Gaṇapatya yogins who are Śiva disciples. No austerity duration stated.

event.details: Śiva teaches ga as all visible/invisible mind-and-speech forms, ṇa as mind/speech-free saṃyoga/ayoga; their Brahmans are principles and nirodha. Both letters are Brahman-forms in Gaṇapati name, and Gaṇeśa their lord. Contemplate mind/speech and their beyond as Gaṇeśa and māyā. He illumines five mind-grounds, hence Cintāmaṇi; worship him as yoga and relinquish grounds for peace. Gaṇeśa transcends saṃyoga/ayoga; abandon māyā-born delusion for happiness. All statements are attributed instruction.

event.details: Bharata reflects that after leaving kingdom and remembering Hari, attachment to deer nevertheless made him deer-bodied. He attributes victory over difficult obstacles by Śiva/Viṣṇu-led gods/all beings to Vighnarāja grace. In time, devoted to Gaṇeśa and meditating on him, he abandons deer body. No new birth narrated within 18 and no express new liberation grant.
